newsitem.title: FRANCE: Lyonnaise says Suez yet to decide on dividend.
newsitem.headline: Lyonnaise says Suez yet to decide on dividend.

text.p: Lyonnaise des Eaux said on Thursday it had not yet fixed terms for a merger with Cie de Suez and warned that any cash payout to sweeten Suez shareholders would be clawed back when share swap parities were fixed.

The comments by Lyonnaise head Jerome Monod suggested a tough behind-the-scenes battle between Suez shareholders, who want to recoup some of the money they have lost on the holding company, and Lyonnaise, which wants to use Suez cash to expand.
Earlier Lyonnaise said its board had unanimously agreed in principle with a planned merger with Suez, due to be discussed at special board meetings of both companies on April 11.

The merger is seen by analysts as a way of giving Lyonnaise access to the Suez cash pile of some five to six billion francs ($0.9-$1.1 billion) -- plus its potential to generate new cash through asset sales -- to fund its own expansion in utilities and telecommunications.
In return Suez, which has had to sell of many key assets to recover from heavy property losses, would gain an identity.
But a call by Suez shareholders for an exceptional dividend to win their backing for the merger has threatened to reduce the cash available to Lyonnaise.
This, warned Monod, would be reflected in any parities fixed for the merger -- suggesting that whatever Suez shareholders got up front in cash, they would lose later in Lyonnaise shares.
"The principle is quite clear. If there is an exceptional dividend payment, it will have an impact on the parity," he told a news conference.
Suez has said it will pay an exceptional dividend to reflect capital gains made on the sale of Banque Indosuez last year but has declined comment on the amount.
On Tuesday Jean-Louis Beffa, head of glassmaker and Suez shareholder Saint-Gobain, suggested Suez pay existing shareholders an amount equivalent to 3.4 billion francs.
Shareholder Generale des Eaux backed Beffa's call on Thursday. Its chairman Jean-Marie Messier told a news conference that "the figure mentioned by Mr Beffa seems to me a reasonable amount".
But it was not clear how much solidarity there was between Suez shareholders on the precise amount of any dividend.
One industry source said a figure had not been discussed between all Suez shareholders. Another said negotiations were still continuing on the amount.
Axa head Claude Bebear, cited by both Beffa and Messier as a supporter of their call, said on Thursday it was up to the Suez board to decide on the merger.
"He (Bebear) does not want to influence the decision of the Suez board, which must take this decision completely calmly," an Axa spokeswoman said.
Monod, who described the idea of a merger as "excellent", said however that detailed talks on merger terms were only now beginning.
"Detailed operational and financial talks about this plan are now starting and we have to wait for the outcome," he said.
"The terms have not been fixed in any way whatsoever."
Earlier Lyonnaise said it made a net attributable profit last year of 1.35 billion francs, compared with 906 million in 1995, on sales of 91.6 billion, up from 85.8 billion.
Its rival Generale des Eaux announced a 1996 net attributable profit of 1.95 billion francs after a loss of 3.69 billion in 1995 on turnover of 166 billion compared to 163 billion.

Lyonnaise shares closed 0.74 percent higher at 542 francs, and Suez shares were down by 0.57 percent at 281 francs while the Paris blue-chip share index closed down 0.62 percent. ($ = 5.631 French Francs)
